source_text:
Ego autem. qui diu multumque iactatus tandem respicere potui, quid sit illa sinceritas, quae sine inanis fabulae narratione percipitur; qui uanas imaginationes animi mei uariis opinionibus erroribusque conlectas uix miser merui domino opitulante conuincere: qui me ad detergendam caliginem mentis tam tarde clementissimo medico uocanti blandientique subieci; qui diu fleui, ut incommutabilis et inmaculabilis substantia concinentibus diuinis libris sese mihi persuadere intrinsecus dignaretur; qui denique omnia illa figmenta, quae uos diuturna consuetudine inplicatos et constrictos tenent, et quaesiui curiose et adtente audiui et temere credidi et instanter, quibus potui, persuasi et aduersus alios pertinaciter animoseque defendi: saeuire in uos omnino non possum, quos sicut me ipsum illo tempore ita nunc debeo sustinere et tanta patientia uobiscum agere. quanta mecum egerunt proximi mei, cum in uestro dogmate rabiosus et caecus errarem.
Ut autem facilius mitescatis et non inimico animo uobisque pernicioso mihi aduersemini, illud quouis iudice inpetrare me oportet a uobis, ut ex utraque parte omnis adrogantia deponatur. nemo nostrum dicat iam se inuenisse ueritatem; sic eam quaeramus, quasi ab utrisque nesciatur. ita enim diligenter et concorditer quaeri poterit, si nulla temeraria praesumptione inuenta et cognita esse credatur. aut si hoc a uobis inpetrare non possum, saltem illud concedite, ut uos tamquam incognitos nunc primum audiam, nunc primum discutiam. iustum puto esse, quod postulo, hac sane lege seruata, ut uobiscum non orem, non conuenticula celebrem.nonManichaei nomen accipiam.sinon mihideomnibus rebus ad salutemanimae pertinentibus sine ulla caligine rationem perspicuam dederitis.
thought_title: Augustine's patience toward Manichaeans and his demand for a fair inquiry
orientation: Augustine is speaking in his own voice, addressing the Manichaeans directly, explaining why he cannot rage against them and setting the terms for a joint search for truth.
pass_a_gloss: But I, who after being tossed about long and much was at last able to look back and see what that sincerity is which is perceived without the telling of an empty story; who barely, wretched as I am, deserved with the Lord's help to refute the empty imaginations of my mind gathered from various opinions and errors; who submitted myself so late to the most merciful physician calling and coaxing me to wipe away the fog of my mind; who wept for a long time that the unchangeable and immaculate substance might deign to persuade me inwardly through the harmonious divine books; who finally sought all those fictions which hold you entangled and bound by long habit, and listened to them attentively, and believed them rashly, and urged them insistently on those I could, and defended them stubbornly and spiritedly against others: I cannot rage against you at all, whom I ought now to endure just as I endured myself at that time, and to deal with you with as much patience as my neighbors dealt with me when I was wandering rabid and blind in your teaching. But so that you may more easily become gentle and not oppose me with a hostile and to yourselves destructive spirit, I must obtain from you this before any judge: that all arrogance be laid aside on both sides. Let none of us say that he has already found the truth; let us seek it as if it were unknown to both parties. For it can be sought diligently and harmoniously only if it is not believed to have been found and known by any rash presumption. Or if I cannot obtain this from you, at least grant this: that you now hear me for the first time as one unknown, now examine me for the first time. I think what I ask is just, with this condition certainly kept: that I do not pray with you, do not attend your assemblies, do not take the name of Manichaean, unless you give me a clear account without any fog concerning all things pertaining to the salvation of the soul.

choices.why: The glossary does not fix this term, but 'sincerity' preserves the sense of purity and freedom from falsehood that Augustine contrasts with 'empty story'.
Renders the phrase literally; 'empty' captures the vanity and lack of substance, and 'imaginations' keeps the mental-image sense without using the glossary term 'fantasies' for phantasmata.
Literal rendering of the superlative; 'physician' is the standard sense of medicus in this metaphor of healing the mind's eye.
Uses the glossary term 'substance' for substantia and literal adjectives; 'immaculate' preserves the negative adjective form.
Literal and forceful; 'rabid' conveys the fury Augustine attributes to his former Manichaean state.
Neutral literal rendering; the diminutive could suggest 'little meetings,' but 'assemblies' is clearer for the Manichaean gatherings.

pass_b_english: But I—after being tossed about for a long time and in many ways, I was at last able to look back and see what that purity is which is grasped without the telling of an empty story; I, who with difficulty and only by the Lord's help, wretched as I was, deserved to refute the empty imaginations of my own mind, gathered together from various opinions and errors; I, who so late submitted myself to the most merciful physician as he called and coaxed me, so that the fog of my mind might be wiped away; I, who wept for a long time so that the unchangeable and immaculate substance might deign to persuade itself to me inwardly, with the divine books joining their voice; I, finally, who both sought out all those fictions carefully that hold you entangled and bound by long habit, and listened to them attentively, and believed them rashly, and persuaded others of them as insistently as I could, and defended them against others stubbornly and passionately—I cannot rage against you at all. whom I must now bear with just as I then bore with myself, and deal with you with as much patience as my neighbors dealt with me, when I was wandering rabid and blind in your teaching.

But so that you may more easily become gentle, and not oppose me with a hostile spirit that is also destructive to yourselves, I must obtain this from you, with any judge you like: that all arrogance be set aside on both sides. Let none of us say that he has already found the truth; let us seek it as if it were unknown to both sides. For it can be sought diligently and harmoniously only if it is not believed by any rash presumption to have already been found and known. Or if I cannot obtain this from you, at least grant me this: that I now hear you for the first time as people unknown to me, and now examine you for the first time. I think what I ask is just, with this condition certainly kept: that I do not pray with you, do not hold assemblies with you, do not take the name of Manichaean—unless you give me a clear account, without any fog, of everything that pertains to the soul's salvation.

problems.why: sinceritas here means purity/clearness, not sincerity

problems.quote: so that the unchangeable and immaculate substance might deign to persuade me from within
problems.source_quote: ut incommutabilis et inmaculabilis substantia concinentibus diuinis libris sese mihi persuadere intrinsecus dignaretur
problems.why: sese mihi persuadere = persuade itself to me, not persuade me; intrinsecus = inwardly, not from within
problems.fix: so that the unchangeable and immaculate substance might deign to reveal itself to me inwardly, with the divine books joining their voice
problems.ruling: 'sese mihi persuadere' = persuade itself to me; 'intrinsecus' = inwardly. 'Persuade me' changes meaning.

problems.why: quibus potui = to whom I could, not on others; persuasi = I persuaded, not urged
problems.fix: and persuaded them as insistently as I could to those I was able
problems.ruling: 'quibus potui' = to whom I could, not 'on others'; 'persuasi' = persuaded, not urged.

problems.quote: Just as my neighbors dealt with me then, so I must now bear with you
problems.source_quote: quos sicut me ipsum illo tempore ita nunc debeo sustinere
problems.why: quos = whom (you), not neighbors; me ipsum = myself, not me then; proximi mei = my neighbors, separate clause
problems.fix: whom I must now bear with just as I then bore with myself, and deal with you with as much patience as my neighbors dealt with me
problems.ruling: 'quos' = whom (you), not neighbors; 'me ipsum' = myself; 'proximi mei' is separate clause.

problems.quote: only if it is not believed
problems.source_quote: si nulla temeraria praesumptione inuenta et cognita esse credatur
problems.why: credatur = it is believed, but nulla...praesumptione = by no rash presumption; missing ablative
problems.fix: if it is not believed, by some rash presumption, to have already been found and known
problems.ruling: Missing ablative 'nulla temeraria praesumptione' = by no rash presumption; changes meaning.

edits.old: so that the unchangeable and immaculate substance might deign to persuade me from within
edits.new: so that the unchangeable and immaculate substance might deign to reveal itself to me inwardly

edits.old: urged them on others as insistently as I could
edits.new: persuaded them as insistently as I could to those I was able

edits.old: Just as my neighbors dealt with me then, so I must now bear with you, and deal with you with as much patience as they dealt with me
edits.new: whom I must now bear with just as I then bore with myself, and deal with you with as much patience as my neighbors dealt with me

edits.old: if it is not believed, by some rash presumption, to have already been found and known
edits.new: if it is not believed by any rash presumption to have already been found and known

fixed: sinceritas here means purity/clearness, not sincerity; changed to purity.
sese mihi persuadere = persuade itself to me, not persuade me; intrinsecus = inwardly, not from within; changed to reveal itself to me inwardly.
quibus potui = to whom I could, not on others; persuasi = I persuaded, not urged; changed to persuaded them as insistently as I could to those I was able.

quos = whom (you), not neighbors; me ipsum = myself, not me then; proximi mei = my neighbors, separate clause; changed to whom I must now bear with just as I then bore with myself, and deal with you with as much patience as my neighbors dealt with me.
credatur = it is believed, but nulla...praesumptione = by no rash presumption; missing ablative; changed to if it is not believed by any rash presumption to have already been found and known.

problems.quote: and believed them rashly, and persuaded them as insistently as I could to those I was able
problems.source_quote: et temere credidi et instanter, quibus potui, persuasi
problems.why: Augustine persuaded others of the fictions, not persuaded the fictions themselves; 'them' is ambiguous/wrong object.
problems.fix: and believed them rashly, and persuaded others of them as insistently as I could
problems.ruling: 'persuasi' takes personal object (quibus potui = people), not 'figmenta'; 'persuaded them' misreads syntax.

problems.why: 'persuadere' means 'to persuade,' not 'to reveal'; the substance deigns to persuade itself to him inwardly.
problems.fix: deign to persuade itself to me inwardly
problems.ruling: 'persuadere' = persuade; 'sese mihi persuadere' = persuade itself to me, not 'reveal itself to me'

edits.old: and believed them rashly, and persuaded them as insistently as I could to those I was able
edits.new: and believed them rashly, and persuaded others of them as insistently as I could

edits.old: might deign to reveal itself to me inwardly
edits.new: might deign to persuade itself to me inwardly

fixed: The source 'et temere credidi et instanter, quibus potui, persuasi' means Augustine believed the fictions rashly and persuaded others of them; the English 'persuaded them... to those I was able' misstates the object, so I changed it to 'persuaded others of them as insistently as I could.'

The source 'sese mihi persuadere intrinsecus dignaretur' uses 'persuadere' with 'sese' as object, meaning the substance deigns to persuade itself to him inwardly; the English 'reveal itself to me' mistranslates 'persuadere,' so I changed it to 'persuade itself to me inwardly.'

problems.quote: and listened to them attentively, and believed them rashly, and persuaded others of them as insistently as I could, and defended them against others stubbornly and passionately—I cannot rage against you at all.
problems.source_quote: et quaesiui curiose et adtente audiui et temere credidi et instanter, quibus potui, persuasi et aduersus alios pertinaciter animoseque defendi: saeuire in uos omnino non possum
problems.why: Source has 'quaesiui curiose' = 'I sought out curiously/carefully'; English omits this adverb.
problems.fix: and sought them out carefully, and listened to them attentively
problems.ruling: Source 'quaesiui curiose' = 'I sought out curiously/carefully' is entirely omitted; 'curiose' meaning lost.

edits.old: who both sought out all those fictions that hold you entangled and bound by long habit, and listened to them attentively
edits.new: who both sought out all those fictions carefully that hold you entangled and bound by long habit, and listened to them attentively

fixed: Added 'carefully' to render 'curiose' from 'et quaesiui curiose et adtente audiui'.

dismissed.quote: and not oppose me with a hostile spirit that is also destructive to yourselves
dismissed.why: Latin says 'not oppose me with a hostile spirit destructive to yourselves AND to me'; English drops 'mihi' (to me).
dismissed.note: 'mihi' is the object of 'aduersemini' (oppose me), not of 'pernicioso', and the English already renders it that way.

dismissed.quote: not take the name of Manichaean—unless you give me
dismissed.why: Missing 'de omnibus rebus' = 'concerning all things'; English omits scope of required account.
dismissed.note: 'Everything that pertains to the soul's salvation' already covers 'de omnibus rebus', and the proposed fix doubles the phrase.
